title: The spoon and the soup (64–68)
hookLine: a fool beside a wise person all his life knows the truth no more than a spoon tastes the soup

lines: A LADLE IN THE POT FOR HOURS.
ONE SIP, AND THE GUEST KNOWS.
cards: A ladle sits in a pot of soup at a family dinner. It's been in there for hours. It has stirred the onions, the broth, the spices, touched every drop.
It's been closer to that soup than anyone at the table, and it has tasted absolutely nothing. Then a guest walks in, takes one spoonful off the ladle, and knows the whole soup in a second.
The Dhammapada puts those two side by side, and asks what makes the difference.

teach.b: Verse sixty-four, in Müller's English: “If a fool be associated with a wise man even all his life, he will perceive the truth as little as a spoon perceives the taste of soup.”
And its twin, verse sixty-five: “If an intelligent man be associated for one minute only with a wise man, he will soon perceive the truth, as the tongue perceives the taste of soup.”
A lifetime next to wisdom, or one minute. The difference isn't how close you are. It's whether you taste.

The commentary tells verse sixty-four about an elder named Udayi who liked to sit in the teacher's seat. Visiting monks assumed he must be learned and asked him questions, and he couldn't answer a single one.
Years near the teaching, like the ladle.
Verse sixty-five goes with a lively story from the monastic rulebook: thirty young men out for a day in the woods with their wives, one of them with a hired companion, who ran off with their things.
Chasing her, they met the Buddha sitting under a tree and asked if he'd seen a woman go by.
He asked them: which is better, to go looking for a woman, or to go looking for yourselves? They sat down to listen. In one conversation, the story says, they understood, and asked to become monks.

Verses sixty-six to sixty-eight add a practical test: a deed is well done when you don't regret it afterward, when you remember it with gladness. So this isn't about being near good things. It's about letting them in.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the spoon-and-soup verses to stress that being near teachers or temples is not the same as taking the teaching in, and to encourage wholehearted listening.

o: a wise teacher who feeds students the truth
a spoon that sits in the soup and tastes nothing
a bowl for serving soup at a monk's meal

games.q: match the pieces of verses sixty-four to sixty-eight.
p: near the soup all its life, tastes nothing
sat in the teacher's seat, couldn't answer

s: being close to a wise person is enough to become wise
the spoon is in the soup all its life and tastes nothing; what matters is tasting.
verse sixty-five says an intelligent person can see the truth in one minute with a wise one
as the tongue tastes the soup.
verses sixty-seven and sixty-eight test a deed by whether you regret it afterward
a deed well done is remembered with gladness.

games.q: you and your friends are chasing someone who ran off with your things. you meet the Buddha under a tree and ask if he's seen her. he answers with a question. what is it?
o: which is better: to look for a woman, or to look for yourselves?
games.why: the young men sat down to listen, understood in one conversation, and asked to become monks: tongue, not spoon.

practice: Take one breath and taste it: the cool at the nostrils, the rise of the chest, the small pause at the top, the long release. All day the breath has gone on unnoticed, like a ladle stirring the pot.
For a couple of minutes, be the tongue: not thinking about breathing, just tasting each one.

wordCard.voice: Dabbi. A spoon, or ladle: one in the soup all its life tastes nothing, while a tongue tastes it in a moment.

orig.note: Pali: spoon or ladle, from verse sixty-four: 'dabbi suparasam yatha,' as a spoon the taste of soup.

carryVoice: Your line: taste the soup. The spoon is near; the tongue tastes. That's day one hundred seventy-two.

sources.q: If a fool be associated with a wise man even all his life, he will perceive the truth as little as a spoon perceives the taste of soup.
If an intelligent man be associated for one minute only with a wise man, he will soon perceive the truth, as the tongue perceives the taste of soup.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 66–68; Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga I.14 (the thirty young men); Dhammapada-atthakatha, stories of Udayi (verse 64) and the thirty (verse 65)
